commitResults.messageTitle: Add greeting and exit messages for AlredTheButtler
Add Alfred banner and fix class name typo
commitResults.messageBody:
Butler was misspelled with a doubled t in the class name, file name and greeting. Also tidy indentation, add Javadoc, and widen the divider to 60 underscores to match the required output format.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Fill in student profile in AGENTS.md
Update README for AlfredTheButler
commitResults.messageBody: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Echo user commands and exit on 'bye'
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a Scanner-based input loop that echoes each command back, and
indent output to match the required sample format.

commitResults.messageTitle: Align output with required transcript format
commitResults.messageBody: Indent message text five spaces and add blank line after each divider.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract message formatting into helper methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Move divider and indent handling into greet() and reply() so the
format is defined once, fixing the greeting indent that the previous
commit missed. Rename variables and update Javadoc.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add task storage and list command
commitResults.messageBody:
Store inputs in a fixed-size String[100] and print them on 'list'.
An array suffices: tasks are capped at 100 and need no persistence.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tidy task list naming and docs
commitResults.messageBody:
Name the task array and its counter, extract the 100-task cap into
MAX_TASKS, and give printList Javadoc explaining its count parameter.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Task class to hold task state
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the String array with Task objects that carry a description
and a done flag, so completion state has somewhere to live. Render
tasks via toString() with an [X] or [ ] status box.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add mark command to complete tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Dispatch 'mark <n>' to Task.markDone(), converting the user's 1-based
number to a 0-based index, and confirm with the updated task. Widen
reply() to varargs so the two-line confirmation and the now-headed
list both reuse one divider block.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add unmark command to reverse done status
commitResults.messageBody:
Dispatch 'unmark <n>' to Task.unmarkDone() and confirm with the
updated task, mirroring the mark command. Extract parseTaskIndex()
so the 1-based to 0-based conversion is defined once for both.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add ToDo task type
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce ToDo, a Task with no date attached, shown with a [T] box in
front of the inherited status box, for example [T][ ] borrow book.
toString delegates the status box back to Task so the done/not-done
format stays defined in one place.

AlfredTheButler now stores each command as a ToDo instead of a plain
Task; command parsing is otherwise unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add deadline command
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce Deadline, a Task with a due time shown as
[D][ ] return book (by: Sunday), and recognise
deadline <description> /by <time> in the command loop. The check runs
before the fallback that turns any other line into a todo, which would
otherwise swallow the whole command as a description.

Confirmations for both task types now share one message showing the
stored task, since the old "added: <line>" echoed the raw command
rather than how it was understood.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add event command
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce Event, a Task with a start and end shown as
[E][ ] project meeting (from: Mon 2pm to: 4pm), and recognise
event <description> /from <start> /to <end> in the command loop.

The search for /to starts after /from, so that a /to appearing inside
the description is not mistaken for the keyword that begins the end
time and split at the wrong place.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Task abstract and trim Javadoc
commitResults.messageBody:
Task can no longer be instantiated on its own now that every task is a
todo, deadline or event, and a bare Task would print without a type
box. Its constructor becomes protected to match.

Drop Javadoc that only restated the code, such as the one-line toString
overrides and the fields behind them, and shorten the main summary that
had grown into a list of every command's syntax. Keep the notes that
explain a decision rather than the code, notably that due times are
stored as typed rather than parsed as dates.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add test-ui skill and text UI test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
The skill compiles the program, replays each case in test/ui-test-plan.md
through a fresh run, and diffs the console output against the expected
output, stopping at the first failure so the failing case is unambiguous.
The plan holds six cases: startup/exit, adding todos, mark and unmark,
deadlines, events, and mixed task types. Every expected output was
captured from a real run rather than written by hand, so indentation and
spacing are exact.

AGENTS.md now requires updating the plan and then running the skill after
each code change. That order matters: running first and adjusting the plan
to match whatever was printed would make the tests agree with bugs.
Also ignore .claude/settings.local.json, which holds machine-local paths.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make the test-ui procedure runnable by agents without skills
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md told the agent to invoke the test-ui skill, which is a no-op
for Codex and any other agent that has no skill mechanism and does not
read .claude/skills. Spell out the fallback: read SKILL.md and follow
its steps directly, since it is only shell commands in Markdown.

Also verified the failure path end to end against a deliberately
regressed build: the run stops at the first failing case and reports the
expected and actual output, leaving later cases unrun.

commitResults.messageTitle: Generalize the test-ui fallback wording
commitResults.messageBody:
Name the real reason the skill can be unavailable - it was added or
edited mid-session and not rescanned yet - instead of naming a specific
agent. The fallback is the same either way: follow SKILL.md by hand, and
never treat a skill that failed to load as a reason to skip the tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how to regenerate shared expected output
commitResults.messageBody:
The greeting banner appears in full in all six expected blocks, so a
rename or banner edit invalidates every one of them. Keeping the blocks
self-contained is only safe if they are regenerated from real runs, so
say that explicitly rather than leaving hand-editing as the obvious path.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record what invalid input actually does today
commitResults.messageBody:
Tried each bad input by hand and wrote down the result, so the gaps are
concrete rather than a vague note that errors are unhandled. Includes one
that was not on the list: an empty line silently adds a task with a blank
description, which does not crash and so is easy to miss.

Re-ran the suite after the edit to confirm the added table does not
disturb case extraction from the plan.

commitResults.messageTitle: Report typing mistakes instead of crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce AlfredException, whose message is shown to the user word for
word, and catch it once in the command loop so a mistake becomes an
ordinary reply and the loop carries on. It is checked rather than
unchecked so that every new rule has to be answered somewhere; a real
bug stays unchecked and still crashes rather than being dressed up as
a polite message.

The first such rule refuses a blank line, which until now was stored as
a task with an empty description - a fault that never crashed and so
was easy to miss. TC7 covers it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parse commands by keyword instead of by prefix
commitResults.messageBody:
Matching prefixes such as "mark " tied the command name to the space
before its arguments, so a command typed without arguments - mark on
its own - did not match its own prefix and was quietly stored as a task
named mark. Take the first word as the command instead, and leave the
rest to whichever command knows how to read it.

Spaces around a line and extra words after a keyword no longer stop a
command being recognised. TC8 covers both, and widens the plan's rule
that input must end with bye, since bye now takes extra words too.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add todo command and refuse unknown keywords
commitResults.messageBody:
Introduce todo <description>, completing the set of commands that add a
task alongside deadline and event, and refuse any keyword Alfred does
not know, naming the word at fault. Only the first word is quoted back,
since repeating a long mistyped line would bury it.

Until now an unrecognised line became a todo described by the whole
line, so a mistyped lst was stored as a task rather than reported. That
fallback is also why todo needed no keyword, so the two changes are
halves of one decision. Cases that added tasks by typing a bare
description now type todo, leaving their expected output unchanged;
TC10 checks that a refused line stores nothing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use American spelling in code comments
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard asks for American spelling in comments, and three
read recognised rather than recognized.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse task commands that are missing parts
commitResults.messageBody:
todo with no description was stored as a task with an empty one, and
deadline or event missing a separator or either of its times crashed
with a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Check that every part is there
and refuse the command with one message naming all the parts it needs.

Match /by, /from and /to without the spaces that used to surround them,
and trim each part afterwards. Spaces baked into the separator made a
missing description indistinguishable from a missing keyword, so
deadline /by Sunday could not be reported for what it is. A well formed
command splits exactly as before, which TC4 and TC5 confirm. TC11 is
new and covers the six ways a part can go missing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check task numbers before using them
commitResults.messageBody:
mark and unmark passed whatever followed the keyword straight to
Integer.parseInt and then to the array, so a word, a missing number, a
zero or a number past the end of the list each crashed in its own way.
Parse and range check the number first, and refuse it with a message.

The range is checked against the number of tasks stored rather than the
length of the array, whose later slots exist but hold null; leaving the
check to the array is what made mark 99 a NullPointerException instead
of an out of bounds. TC12 covers both messages and every route to them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store tasks in an ArrayList instead of an array
commitResults.messageBody:
The task array was fixed at 100 slots and needed a separate taskCount
alongside it, since an array cannot report how much of itself is in
use. A 101st task would have overrun it.

Use an ArrayList, which grows as needed and knows its own size, so
MAX_TASKS and taskCount both go away. Nothing printed changes: TC1 to
TC12 pass untouched, which is what shows the swap was behavior neutral.
The array overrun is dropped from the plan's known gaps, since the list
closes it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add delete command
commitResults.messageBody:
A task could be added but never removed, so one typed by mistake stayed
in the list for good.

Add delete <number>, confirming with the task removed and the count
left. It reads its number through parseTaskIndex, the helper mark and
unmark already share, so a bad number is refused with the existing
messages rather than new ones. Removing from the list shifts the later
tasks down, so the list stays numbered from 1 with no gap. TC13 is new
and covers that renumbering; TC12 gains two delete lines to show the
number is checked before anything is removed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Look up commands through an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
The command keywords were seven String constants that the main switch
matched by value. A misspelled case label was silently dead code rather
than a compile error, and the unknown-command message sat in the switch's
default arm, away from the keywords it was refusing.

Replace them with a Command enum that pairs each command with its keyword
and looks one up by keyword, throwing AlfredException when none matches.
The switch now runs over enum constants and needs no default arm. What
the program prints is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Apply se-edu style guidelines to code and docs
Add style-check and commit-check skills
commitResults.messageBody:
The project follows four style and convention guides, and keeping to
them was a manual effort that depended on remembering to do it.

Add two skills that check against those guides, and mandate both in
AGENTS.md so they run as part of finishing a change rather than on
request. Both fetch their guides from the source URLs on every run
instead of embedding a copy, so they follow the guides as they stand
and report honestly when a guide cannot be read.

commitResults.messageTitle: Save tasks to disk whenever the list changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks live only in memory, so they are lost when the program exits.
Write the whole list to data/alfred.txt after every command that
changes it; rewriting rather than appending lets one method cover
adding, marking, and deleting alike, and cannot leave the file
half-updated.

Reading the file back at startup is not implemented yet, so saved
tasks do not reappear on the next run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load saved tasks at startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are written to data/alfred.txt but never read, so a restart
starts from an empty list. Read the file before the first command,
and report how many tasks came back when there are any.

The test harness now clears the save file between cases, which is what
keeps them independent, and supports two-run cases that check what
survives a restart.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle edge cases in saving, loading, and input
commitResults.messageBody:
A description containing the field separator is cut short when saved,
one damaged line costs the whole list, and input ending without bye
throws instead of exiting. Escape the separator, skip only the lines
that cannot be read, treat the end of the input as bye, and make
counts read "1 task" rather than "1 tasks".

Move line assembly into Storage so the escaping and unescaping cannot
drift apart, and route test harness blocks by label, so a case can
seed a damaged save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the save folder as its own path constant
commitResults.messageBody:
Asking the save file for its parent breaks if that path is ever a bare
filename, which has none. Name the folder separately instead, and
delete the whole folder between test cases so every case starts from
what a fresh copy of the project finds.

commitResults.messageTitle: Correct and trim stale Javadoc
Merge branch 'branch-level-7'
Add a comment-check skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Comments go stale as code moves, and nothing in the build notices.
Correcting them is a manual pass done from memory.

Add a skill that finds stale and redundant comments across
src/main/java and proposes removals for approval, rather than
deleting on its own: a deleted comment takes with it information the
code does not hold. Lean on javac -Xdoclint for the cases a compiler
can prove, and keep the threshold conservative, since AGENTS.md asks
for comments rather than merely allowing them.

commitResults.messageTitle: commit-check: Add and correct message checks
commitResults.messageBody:
Using the skill on its own commit surfaced two defects in it, and
the guide states a rule the skill did not check.

Warn when the body hedges its description of the situation with
either of the two terms the guide names. Apply the capitalization
rule to the part after any scope prefix, so that the guide's own
`bug fix: Add space after name` example no longer fails. Look for
the hedging terms in the body alone: a subject naming them matched
itself.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store deadline and event times as dates
commitResults.messageBody:
The times of a deadline and an event were kept as whatever words the
user typed, so the program could not tell which day was meant. Reading
them into a LocalDate is what later lets them be compared or shown in
another format.

Only the yyyy-mm-dd form is understood, and a time that is not a date
has no message of its own yet. Storage turns a bad date into an
AlfredException so that one hand-edited line is skipped rather than
costing the whole save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show task dates as MMM dd yyyy
commitResults.messageBody:
A date was shown in the yyyy-mm-dd form it was typed and saved in, which
reads as a serial number rather than as a day. Showing it as Oct 15 2019
is the point of having stored a real date rather than the user's words.

The save file keeps yyyy-mm-dd, since that is the form that reads back
exactly. The formatter is pinned to English so a month name does not
change with the computer the program runs on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test edge-case dates through the save round trip
commitResults.messageBody:
The round trip through the save file was covered only by TC14, whose
dates are ordinary ones. A single-digit month, a leap day, and a year
boundary are where a mismatch between the file's format and the
displayed one would show first, and none of them was exercised.

Add TC20 to cover the three. No program change was needed: the dates
already survive, checked here and separately against every day of four
years.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse a bad date with a message
commitResults.messageBody:
A date the program could not read reached LocalDate.parse unchecked and
came back through the safety net meant for bugs, which replied with the
name of a Java class. That is no help to someone who typed the date.

Read dates in DateParser instead, shared by the commands and the save
file so the two cannot disagree about what a date is. It tells apart the
two ways a date is wrong, since the reader can act on each differently:
the wrong format is answered with the right one, an impossible day with
a pointer at the day and the month.

Also refuse an event that ends before it starts, which is readable on
both ends and still describes nothing that can happen.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an on command to show one day's tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Storing real dates was worth little while nothing asked a question of
them. The list could only be read whole, so finding what falls on a day
meant scanning it by eye.

Ask each task whether it falls on the day, rather than testing what kind
it is: a deadline answers for its due day, an event for every day it
spans, and a task with no date answers no. The decision then sits beside
the dates it is made from, and a new kind of task cannot be forgotten.

Number the matches by their place in the whole list, not from 1. The
other commands count through the whole list, so a number shown here has
to be the one they expect; renumbering would make mark act on a task the
user cannot see.

Move the display format in beside the format dates are read in, so that
both forms sit together and Task goes back to being about tasks. Rename
DateParser to Dates now that it does more than parse: asking a parser to
format read as a contradiction at every call site.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clean up stale Javadoc
Remove a pass-through method from Storage
commitResults.messageBody:
parseDate did nothing but call Dates.parse. What justified it was its
comment, explaining why a bad date has to raise a checked exception:
load skips a damaged line by catching one, and an unchecked exception
would escape with the rest of the file unread. That reasoning now sits
on load, where the catch it describes actually is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
Extract a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
The main class decided what to do about a command and also owned every
detail of how the answer looked: the dividers, the indent, the banner,
and the wording of each reply. Those are separate concerns, and mixing
them meant the command loop could not be read without reading the
formatting too.

Gathering them in one class puts the shape of a reply in one place, and
leaves the loop saying what to tell the user rather than how it appears
on screen. Reading commands moves there as well, since both ends of the
conversation go through the console. Nothing the program prints changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Deciding what a line means and deciding what to do about it were the
same code. The loop was mostly string handling — finding /by, checking
for an empty description, turning a typed number into an index — with
the actual decisions buried inside it.

Gathering that in one class leaves the loop reading as a list of
commands, and puts every refusal the user can provoke by mistyping in
one file, where the wording can be kept consistent. A line is read once
and yields both its command and its arguments together, so the two
cannot come from different lines. Nothing the program prints changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a TaskList class
commitResults.messageBody:
The tasks were a bare list passed from hand to hand, so anything holding
it could do anything to it. Marking a task read as tasks.get(i).markDone
-- two steps into someone else's data to express one idea -- and the
list could be changed by anyone it was handed to, including the code
that only meant to save it.

Giving the list a class of its own lets callers ask for what they want
rather than reach in and take it. The operations that act on a stored
task hand that task back, since each is followed by showing the user
what was affected, and fetching it again after a delete would find the
wrong one. Nothing the program prints changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make the chatbot an object
commitResults.messageBody:
A run was a static main method, so the four parts it works with were
locals threaded through it, and there was no way to have two chatbots
saving to different files. Storage also chose its own save file, which
left the class that does the saving deciding where to save.

Give the chatbot a constructor taking the save file, fields for the
parts, and a run method holding the loop, so that main is one line.
Loading stays in run rather than the constructor: it has something to
tell the user, and saying it from a constructor would put it before the
greeting. Nothing the program prints changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the task list check its own indices
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser decided whether a number named a real task, which meant it
had to be told how many tasks there were: reading a piece of text took a
parameter about the state of the list. The list, meanwhile, took every
index on trust and would have thrown a fault of its own had a bad one
ever reached it.

Move that half of the check to the list, which is the only thing that
knows its own size, and leave the parser deciding only whether the text
is a number at all. Walking the list for display still takes its index
on trust, since those are made from the size rather than typed. Both
refusals keep their wording, so nothing the program prints changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make each command a class of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
The loop was a switch over every keyword, so it knew what all nine
commands do and had to be edited to add a tenth. Two locals carried
results back out of the switch -- a task to store, a flag saying the
list had changed -- which is a sign the arms were being cut off before
they had finished their work.

Give each command a class with an execute method, and have the parser
build one rather than name one. A command now finishes its own job,
saving when it has changed something, so the flag has nothing to say
and the loop no longer knows what any command does. The enum goes: a
keyword now turns into an object rather than into a switch label.

End of input builds the same exit command that bye does, which puts the
parting message in one place instead of two.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix three comments that had gone wrong
Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
Organize the classes into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class sat in the default package, which said nothing about which
classes belong together and left them unimportable from any named
package.

Group them under alfred, with alfred.command for the eight command
classes and alfred.task for the five task classes. Those two are the
only closed families, and the only places a new class gets added. Ui,
Parser, Storage, and the two classes the whole program leans on stay in
alfred rather than in packages of one.

The test-ui skill and the README named the main class and the source
glob by their old paths, so both are updated.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tighten visibility now that packages exist
commitResults.messageBody:
Every member was public because the default package left no other
option. Packages make it possible to say which members are meant for
use elsewhere and which are internal.

Drop to package-private or private what nothing outside uses: the
helpers Parser.parse is built from, Parser.parse and Dates.parse, the
Storage constructor with load and its result record, and the seven Ui
methods only the command loop calls. Ui is where this says the most:
what stays public is what a command uses to report a result, while
reading input and reporting an error stay with the loop.

Task.markDone and unmarkDone stay public as a pair, since Storage
calls the first, and the AlfredTheButler constructor and run() stay
public as the documented way to start a chatbot.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
commitResults.messageBody:
The project is built by invoking javac and java by hand, which leaves
the JDK version, the classpath and the output layout to be set up
again on every machine it is cloned to.

Bring in the Gradle build supplied with the course template. The build
is described once in build.gradle, and the checked-in wrapper pins the
Gradle version and fetches it on demand, so a clone needs no separate
Gradle install.

The branch forked off before the source was moved into packages, so
its build.gradle still names the template's main class. Running the
app through Gradle needs that pointed at the real one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add unit tests for date parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates.parse takes a string and returns a date, with no console output,
no file access, and no task list behind it, so it can be tested with no
setup at all. That makes it the natural method to cover first.

Assert on the message for the two failing groups, not only on the
exception type: both throw AlfredException, and telling a wrong format
apart from a date that names no real day is what the class exists to do.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix main class name in build script
commitResults.messageBody:
The application block still named seedu.duke.Duke, left over from the
template, so gradle run failed on a class that does not exist. The
entry point is alfred.AlfredTheButler.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add unit tests for date formatting
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates.format is the other method in the class that can be tested on its
own terms: a date goes in, text comes out, with nothing else behind it.

Cover a non-English default locale as well. Dates pins the month name
to English on purpose, so that a task reads the same on every machine,
and a change that undid the pin would look harmless in the diff.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add unit tests for parsing, storage, and tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Cover the methods where a fault would be both likely and quiet: the
task number, which is converted from the user's counting to the list's
and would otherwise act on the neighboring task; the escaping that
lets any description survive the save file; and the index checks that
stand between a mistyped number and an unchecked exception.

Leave Ui and the command loop out. Both only print, and the text UI
tests already check what they print, so unit tests over captured
streams would restate that at more cost than it is worth.

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Add a unit test coverage target
commitResults.messageBody:
The instructions cover style and the text UI tests but say nothing
about JUnit, so a change can leave the suite behind with nothing to
catch it.

Set the target at the more valuable half of the methods, and say how
to rank them and how to report the split. The number alone does not
say which half to pick, and there is no coverage tool here to settle
it. Ask for the tests to be brought back into line after every change
under src/main/java, in the same shape as the text UI steps below.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
Name the fat JAR after the app and document it
commitResults.messageBody:
The shadowJar output kept the name duke.jar from the template, which
does not match this chatbot.

Add a README section on building, locating, and running the JAR, since
nothing recorded how to distribute the app.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Jar'
Fill the gaps in the generated Javadoc
commitResults.messageBody:
Nearly every class and method already carries a header comment, but
the generated documentation still has holes a reader meets first: the
three package summary pages are blank, and six classes show a
constructor with no description, since Java supplies one implicitly
when none is written.

Give each package an overview of what it holds and how its classes
relate, and write those constructors out so they can be described.
Dates and Parser take private ones: neither holds state, so nothing
has reason to instantiate them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the coding standard on cases and constants
commitResults.messageBody:
The se-edu Java conventions indent the labels of a switch one level
in from the switch, and ask associated constants to share a prefix
rather than a suffix. Parser and Storage break both.

Let's indent the case labels, and rename BY_SEPARATOR to SEPARATOR_BY
and TODO_FIELDS to FIELDS_TODO, with their two groups, so each set
sorts and reads together. Every renamed constant is private, so
nothing outside these two classes changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the se-edu Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The conventions reach the code only through style-check, which fetches
them once a file has been written. A rule that arrives after the
writing costs an edit, a rebuild, and a test run to apply.

Let's write the conventions out in a seedu-java-coding-standard skill,
so they can be applied while typing, and mandate it in AGENTS.md for
every Java file rather than for src/main/java alone. The tests are
Java too, and were never exempt in principle. style-check keeps the
Markdown and prose guides and defers the Java ones here, so one guide
does not have two owners.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the se-edu Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
The conventions reach a message only through commit-check, which
fetches them once the message is drafted. A rule that arrives after
the drafting costs a rewrite, and cannot be applied at all once the
commit is pushed.

Let's write the conventions out in a seedu-git-standard skill, so they
can be applied while drafting, and leave commit-check the workflow
around one message: the draft, the approval, and the amend.

The branch rule needs an exception. The course prescribes the names
branch-A-CodingStandard and branch-Level-7, which are not kebab case
and cannot be made so, and a check that fails on every increment
branch is one a reader learns to ignore.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove the commit-check skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Every section of commit-check now exists in seedu-git-standard: the
draft file, the checks, the approval, the local rules, and the amend
against an unpushed commit. What is left of it is indirection.

Let's remove it, and point AGENTS.md and the standard at each other
directly. Two skills over one guide is how the two come to disagree.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command
commitResults.messageBody:
A list only stays useful if a task can be found in it, so add
find <keyword>, which shows the tasks whose description contains the
keyword. The search ignores case, since someone searching for a word
means the word rather than one spelling of it.

Matches keep their number from the whole list, the way the on command
already numbers them, so that a number shown by find is the one mark,
unmark, and delete act on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Checkstyle to the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The se-edu Java conventions are enforced only by the coding standard
skill, which runs when it is invoked rather than on every build, so
code edited outside that path can drift without anything noticing.

Let's add the Checkstyle Gradle plugin with the rule set from
AddressBook Level 3, which encodes the same conventions. The plugin
attaches to the check task, so a build now fails on a violation.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CheckStyle'
Add JavaFX to the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has no GUI toolkit on its classpath, so the graphical
version of Alfred that follows cannot compile.

Let's add the JavaFX dependencies. The jars for all three operating
systems are listed rather than this machine's alone, so that the
project still builds and runs for someone working on another one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a graphical window for Alfred
commitResults.messageBody:
Alfred is a console program, so using it means running a terminal and
reading its replies line by line.

Let's add a JavaFX window, laid out as part 2 of the JavaFX tutorial
describes: a scrolling list of dialog boxes above a text field and a
Send button, each message shown beside the avatar of whoever said it.
The user's messages take the left of the conversation and Alfred's the
right, so that the two sides can be told apart at a glance.

The window is a layout and nothing else. Typing in it does nothing,
since nothing listens to the text field or the button yet, and the
console program is unchanged. The window does become what "gradlew
run" starts, so the console program is reached by running its class
directly, which is how the text UI tests already run it.

Those tests compile every source with javac, which now needs the
JavaFX jars, so the build gained a task that prints the classpath and
the test-ui skill hands it to javac. The two avatars are placeholders,
meant to be replaced by real pictures.

commitResults.messageTitle: Respond to what the user types in the window
commitResults.messageBody:
The window shows a greeting and nothing else. Neither the text field
nor the Send button is wired to anything, so a line typed into the
window disappears the moment it is sent.

Let's echo each line back as a dialog box of the user's own. Both ways
of sending a line share one handler: a mouse click on the button, and
the text field's own action event, which is what Enter fires there.

A dialog box added to a full pane sits below the bottom of the view,
so the pane scrolls to the end whenever the container's height
changes, keeping the newest message in sight.

Alfred still does not answer. Connecting the window to the part of the
program that reads commands comes next.

commitResults.messageTitle: Answer the lines sent from the window
commitResults.messageBody:
A line sent from the window is shown and left there. The window has
nowhere to get an answer from, since the only way into the chatbot is
the command loop, which reads the console and writes to it.

Let's give AlfredTheButler a getResponse method for the window to call,
and show what it returns as a dialog box of Alfred's beside the user's
own. The answer echoes the line back for now, so that the exchange is
settled in one step and the wiring to the commands in another.

Creating the chatbot from the window also wants a constructor that
takes no save file, since the window has no more reason to choose one
than main does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Flip the dialog boxes that belong on the left
commitResults.messageBody:
A dialog box decides its own direction: the constructor takes a flag
saying whose box it is, and branches on it twice, once for the
alignment and once for the order of the children. Everything else
about a box is the same either way, so the two arrangements sit apart
in the one place they have in common.

Let's build every box facing right and give it a flip method for the
ones that belong on the left. The direction then lives in a method of
its own, the constructor is left with what it shares, and the two
static methods that name the speakers keep the choice away from the
window.

Nothing about the window changes: the same snapshot comes out of it,
pixel for pixel.

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe the dialog box layout in FXML
commitResults.messageBody:
A dialog box builds itself in Java: the label, the picture, their
sizes and the alignment are all statements in a constructor. Reading
what a box looks like means reading code, and changing it means
rebuilding the program to see the result.

Let's move the arrangement into view/DialogBox.fxml and leave the
class with what the file cannot say: which words and picture a box is
given, and which way round it faces. A box loads that file as its own
root and controller, so it is still created like an ordinary object
and nothing outside it needs to know an FXML file is involved.

The layout gained the padding and the 99-pixel avatars the tutorial
specifies, so the boxes sit further apart than before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load the main window from FXML
commitResults.messageBody:
Main builds the window itself: it creates every control, sizes and
places each one, hangs the handlers off two of them, and holds the
images and the chatbot besides. Everything the window is and
everything it does sit in one method, so neither can be found without
reading past the other.

Let's describe the window in view/MainWindow.fxml and put what happens
in it in MainWindow, a controller the loader fills in by name. Main is
left with the little that has to happen before there is a window at
all: read the layout, put it on the stage, and hand the window the
chatbot to ask.

The pane still follows the newest message down by way of a listener.
The tutorial binds the scroll position to the height of the
conversation instead, but a bound position cannot be set by anything
else, and scrolling up to read what was said earlier is something else
setting it.

The window keeps the title and the fixed size the layout file has
nothing to say about.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the window's controls follow its edges
commitResults.messageBody:
The controls sit where the layout file puts them, so the window is
kept at one size to stop them being left behind. A conversation is
then read four hundred pixels wide whether or not there is room for
more.

Let's anchor each control to the edges it should follow: the text
field to the left, right and bottom, the Send button to the bottom
right corner, and the pane to all four. The window can then be
resized, and the smallest size it allows is the one below which the
conversation and the text field stop being usable.

commitResults.messageTitle: Style the window with CSS
commitResults.messageBody:
The window is JavaFX's default grey, and a message is a bare label
against it. Nothing marks a message off from the one below it, or
tells the two speakers apart beyond which side they sit on.

Let's give the window a stylesheet and the dialog boxes one of their
own, so that a message reads as a bubble and the window has a colour
of its own. The flipped box takes an extra style class, because the
corner a bubble leaves square is the one nearest its owner, and that
corner moves with the box.

The stylesheets are named by the layout files that use them, which is
what Scene Builder writes when a stylesheet is linked there.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ui: Collect a reply instead of printing it
commitResults.messageBody:
Every message the Ui has goes to standard output. A window has no
standard output to read, so as things stand the only way to put a
reply in a dialog box would be to build the reply somewhere else, and
then the window and the console would each have their own wording to
keep right.

Let's give the Ui a mode in which it collects what it is told to say
and hands it back. Every reply already goes through one method, so
the mode is one branch there rather than one per message, and the
console path is left exactly as it was.

A collected reply carries no dividers and no indent. Those mark a
block off from the rest of a console session, and a dialog box marks
itself off. The banner is left out for the same kind of reason: it is
drawn out of characters lined up in columns, which needs the
fixed-width font a console has and a window does not.

Nothing calls this yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Answer the window with the real commands
commitResults.messageBody:
The window echoes. Alfred answers a line with the words back again,
so the task list can be reached by typing at a console and no other
way, and the window is a picture of a chatbot rather than one.

Let's answer the window from the commands themselves. getResponse
parses a line, carries it out and returns what the Ui collected, with
the same two refusals the loop makes; getGreeting does what the loop
does before it starts. The commands, the parser and the task list are
untouched and cannot tell the two interfaces apart.

Reading the save file is part of the greeting rather than an errand
of the window's, and it matters as much as answering does: a window
that had not read it would answer the first command against an empty
list and save that over the tasks on disk.

The line is trimmed before it is parsed. The parser is handed a
trimmed line by contract, and the console trims what it reads, but a
window hands over its text field exactly as it stands; without this a
stray space would leave a command unrecognized in the window alone.

Typing bye no longer ends anything, since there is no loop to end. It
is answered like any other command, and the window is the user's to
close.

commitResults.messageTitle: Color a reply by the command it answers
commitResults.messageBody:
Every reply looks the same. A glance down the conversation says who
spoke and nothing else, so finding where a task was added or deleted
means reading the replies one by one.

Let's color the bubble by the kind of command the reply answers,
which the chatbot now remembers and the window asks for: yellow for
adding, palegreen for marking, lightpink for deleting. Marking and
unmarking share a color, being two halves of the same act.

A line that named no command leaves the bubble alone. Two of them
exist: a refused line, and anything said before the first command.
The tutorial's version keeps the previous kind after a refusal and so
colors the refusal by it, and hands its switch a null before the
first command, which throws where the window cannot catch it.

The window also takes the backdrop as its background.

commitResults.messageTitle: README: Describe the window as well as the console
commitResults.messageBody:
The README knows one program. It says to run AlfredTheButler.main, or
the JAR, and to expect the banner as the output. The JAR opens the
window now, so a reader who follows it is promised something the
program no longer does.

Let's describe both forms and how to start each. The console version
still prints what the README shows; it is reached by naming its class
rather than by running the JAR, and both forms keep their tasks in the
same file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-10'
Build save fields and task lists with varargs
commitResults.messageBody:
Each kind of task built the fields every task shares and then pushed
its type letter in at the front, and TaskList had a no-arg constructor
beside a List one. A varargs parameter lets a subclass name its fields
once, in the order they are saved, and lets one constructor cover a
list of no tasks as well as a list of several.

toFileFields becomes abstract as a result: with the type letter
supplied per kind there is no shared answer left to inherit. The List
constructor stays, since tasks read back from the save file arrive as
a list. Neither the file format nor anything the program prints
changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Varargs'
Trim Javadoc rationale and fix stale comments
commitResults.messageBody:
The Javadoc under src/main/java had grown to 1449 comment lines against
937 of code. Three quarters of that was rationale, and much of it went
past the reason for a decision into the alternatives that were rejected,
which the diff and the code already show.

Condense those passages to the reason itself, and drop paragraphs whose
point is already in the summary above them. Keep the ones that head off
a misreading: escaping the escape character first, numbering matches by
their place in the whole list, and why a launcher class exists at all.

Three comments had also gone stale when find was added at Level 9. The
command list in run(), and the list of commands that save nothing in the
command package summary, both omitted it. The alfred package summary
claimed AlfredTheButler holds the command loop and nothing else, which
stopped being true once the window gained getGreeting and getResponse.

No executable line changes, so the tests and the UI test plan are
untouched.

commitResults.messageTitle: Punctuate Javadoc tags and clarify vague names
commitResults.messageBody:
A peer review of PR #529 raised two rules the code was breaking. The
se-edu conventions ask for punctuation behind every parameter
description, and 156 tag descriptions across main and test had none.
They also ask that associated constants share a common prefix, and the
four date constants in Dates did not.

Add a period to the end of every @param, @return and @throws
description, on the last line where one spans several.

Rename the Dates constants around the distinction they were hiding.
The class holds two formats, one for dates as they are typed and saved
and one for dates as they are shown, so FORMAT, EXAMPLE and SHAPE become
DATE_INPUT_FORMAT, DATE_INPUT_EXAMPLE and DATE_INPUT_SHAPE, and
DISPLAY_FORMAT becomes DATE_DISPLAY_FORMAT. All four then share a
prefix, and each says which of the two forms it belongs to. The review
suggested DATE_FORMAT for the first; that would have left the display
constant unprefixed and the question of which form it serves unanswered.

Rename three locals named for what happened to them rather than for what
they hold: loaded to loadResult, escaped to escapedFields, and tmp to
reversedChildren. The review named the first; the other two are the same
mistake in other files.

Values and control flow are untouched, so the tests and the UI test plan
need no change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Enforce Javadoc tag punctuation in the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The punctuation rule was in the coding standard skill's rules from the
start, but only in its reading pass, where judgment is applied rather
than a pattern. It was read past twice and reported clean both times,
and a peer review then found it broken on 156 tags. A rule left to
attention holds only until attention lapses.

Add a checkJavadocTagPunctuation task and wire it into check, so the
build refuses what a skill only reports. Checkstyle has no module for
this, and a single-line pattern cannot do it either: a description may
wrap onto the lines below it and the period belongs at the end of the
last one, so the task reads the whole tag. Breaking a single-line tag
and the last line of a wrapped one confirms it fails on both, and that a
continuation line without a period is not mistaken for a violation.

Add the two Checkstyle modules that cover neighboring ground,
NonEmptyAtclauseDescription and RequireEmptyLineBeforeBlockTagGroup.

Audit the rest of the rules for the same gap. Test method naming and the
third-person verb a method summary opens with were both checkable and
unchecked, so add them to the mechanical pass. Constant prefixes stay a
reading-pass item, since which constants are associated is a judgment a
pattern cannot make.

Record the principle in the skill: a rule a pattern can see belongs in
the mechanical pass, and a check that misses what a person catches is
fixed by adding the check, not by resolving to read more carefully.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix inert style checks and the switch indent rule
commitResults.messageBody:
Several checks in the Java coding standard skill could never fail:
this platform's grep ignores \s, \w, and \b in an ERE, and awk reads
\b as a backspace. They reported clean over code that was violating
them fourteen times, so the skill now warns about both traps and
asks for a new check to be proven against a real violation first.

The skill's switch rule also contradicted the se-edu guide, which
aligns each case with the switch instead of indenting it. The guide
wins, so Checkstyle enforces caseIndent 0 and the existing switches
follow.
